A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the MULTITP study, despite the changed title and substantially revised analyses. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM preference measurements, reason classifications, and language-specific capability and consistency results in Sections 5–6 and Appendices D–E.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 19 LLMs, language clustering, correlation analyses, and paraphrase robustness results in Section 5 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: The core MULTITP construction and prompting approach remains: controlled trolley scenarios, automatic translation, and forced-choice completion. The prompt called token-forcing in v2 already appears in v1 Section 4.3. New scoring and analysis procedures change evaluation rather than establish a new model or inference method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same trolley-problem domain, six moral dimensions, random-character scenarios, and Moral Machine human reference data. Appendix B.1 contains the same 107 language codes in both versions; v1's references to 106 do not establish narrower coverage. Paraphrases test the retained task within existing languages.

E2.justification: v1 Table 4 compares nine GPT variants; v2 Figure 2 compares 19 models, adding Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen, and GPT-4o Mini. Older GPT variants and GPT-3.5 disappear from the reported preference comparisons, although GPT-3.5 remains in v2's API documentation table.

E3.justification: v2 introduces global speaker-weighted model scoring, language-sensitivity measurement, four-cluster analysis, and a five-paraphrase evaluation on 14 languages using Llama 3 8B and 70B. The latter adds agreement, kappa, F1, and accuracy metrics. The underlying L2 distance and zero-temperature decoding were already present in v1.

E4.justification: v1's character-level preference analysis, reason decomposition, answer-eligibility analysis, order-consistency results, and extended response case studies are removed. v2 adds model-specific language clustering, analyses of dimensions associated with misalignment, speaker-count correlations, and paraphrase robustness tests. These substantially replace the questions investigated by the supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports descriptive frequencies without inferential uncertainty assessment. v2 adds Pearson correlations with significance reporting for moral dimensions and speaker counts, including coefficients and p-values for all 19 models in Table 10. It also newly states that generation uses a fixed random seed. Neither version establishes repeated-run uncertainty estimates or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v1's reason-distribution results, including GPT-4's 52.72% utilitarianism and 41.85% fairness, disappear. v2 newly reports three Llama models with global misalignment below 0.6, near-zero speaker-count correlations, and paraphrase results of 75.9% four-of-five agreement, 78% F1, and 81% accuracy. Its world map evaluates Llama 3.1 70B instead of GPT-4, so this is a replacement result rather than a same-model improvement.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5.3 introduces a formal definition of cross-language sensitivity using dispersion of language-specific preferences. The displayed L2 misalignment equation otherwise formalizes the distance already described in v1 Appendix D. Neither version contains substantial theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes language inequality and GPT-3/GPT-4 differences in dominant moral justifications. v2 removes the justification claims and foregrounds generally weak human alignment across 19 models. It also redefines the inequality question around high- versus low-resource languages and concludes that systematic disadvantage is not demonstrated, rather than treating cross-language differences themselves as inequality.

C2.justification: Interpretations of utilitarianism/fairness shifts and language-specific comprehension failures give way to explanations involving preference diversity, influential moral dimensions, and speaker-count correlations. v2 newly argues that procedural generation avoids training exposure when interpreting those correlations. It also expands discussion of dimension-dependent refusals and the limits of treating trolley-task alignment as real-world moral competence.

D1.justification: v2 adds open-model checkpoint identifiers and VRAM requirements, five exact paraphrases, dataset statistics, translation-checking information, and details of demographic-source collection and first-language weighting. Conversely, v1's explicit system-role prompt and full response transcripts disappear. The code/data link is retained. Some documentation remains inconsistent, including the vignette total and model identifiers.

R1.justification: v2 substantially reframes the study around pluralistic alignment and psychological evaluation, explicitly distinguishes it from Takemoto's Moral Machine LLM study, and expands Table 1 with MoCa, GlobalOpinionQA, OffTheRails, and PRISM. It also recognizes controlled variation in MoralExceptQA, qualifying v1's stronger contrast with prior datasets. Literature supporting the removed moral-reason categories is dropped.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, dataset exposition, and conclusions are extensively rewritten. The results narrative becomes five research questions with separate methods and findings, replacing the moral-tendencies/meta-behaviors organization. The appendices are substantially reorganized, and the extended multilingual-example appendix is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. Reason-decomposition charts and capability histograms are replaced by ranked bars, violin plots, radar plots, and cluster boxplots, with several new tables. Figure 1 is reformatted, and the world map moves to the appendix with a different model, scale, and legend.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis for general claims about LLM alignment: v1's GPT-centered comparisons and descriptive language examples are supplemented or replaced by comparisons across multiple model families, explicit speaker-count tests, and quantified prompt robustness. These address important weaknesses in generality and evidential support, while checkpoint documentation improves reproducibility. The loss of detailed rationale analyses is a meaningful tradeoff. Dataset/model documentation inconsistencies remain, and null correlations do not prove equal alignment, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evaluation.
